section_summary: This section begins with recovered Japanese Legation records from Panama, then documents U.S. efforts to locate, preserve, examine, and dispose of Japanese diplomatic archives and property after Japan’s surrender. Reports from Haiti, Romania, Thailand, Venezuela, Panama, Canada, and Chile describe destroyed archives, confiscated equipment, funds, real estate, vehicles, furniture, and procedures for Allied custody. The section ends with a translated installment of former Japanese Minister Yamagata’s 1942 diary, detailing Chilean politics, Axis diplomatic coordination, intelligence activity, financial controls, propaganda, and concern over a possible break with Japan.

subfiles.title: Material from the Japanese Legation in Panama: personal and registration records
subfiles.doc_type: Recovered Japanese legation records and identification cards
subfiles.from: Japanese Legation, Panama
subfiles.about: Recovered Japanese-language personnel and registration records contain names, dates, addresses, and official annotations from Panama and neighboring countries.
subfiles.summary: These fragmentary, heavily degraded cards were marked as material from the Japanese Legation in Panama, mostly on September 21–22, 1945. They include Japanese names, biographical entries, dates, addresses in Panama, Caracas, and Colombia, and earlier consular or administrative stamps.

subfiles.title: Japanese diplomatic property and nationals in Haiti
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Port-au-Prince (Orme Wilson)
subfiles.about: Reports that Haiti had no Japanese diplomatic mission, assets, or known Japanese nationals.
subfiles.summary: Haiti: no Japanese diplomatic mission ever existed and the Embassy knows of no Japanese assets or nationals; an honorary consul's records were examined in an earlier despatch.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 719: Report on Japanese Archives and Records
subfiles.from: Burton Y. Berry, U.S. Mission, Bucharest
subfiles.about: Reports the Allied seizure of Japanese Embassy and military-attaché property in Romania and the absence of diplomatic archives.
subfiles.summary: Allied Control Commission representatives opened sealed Japanese premises in Bucharest and confiscated the property found there. Romanian and Swedish sources reported that the Japanese archives had been burned and most state property sold in 1944; some household goods were left for interned Japanese officials at Ghencea.

subfiles.title: Statement on opening the Japanese military attaché’s rooms
subfiles.from: Allied Control Commission and Romanian officials
subfiles.about: Records the opening of rooms at 36 Boulevard Alexandru Constantinescu and the removal of Japanese military-attaché property.
subfiles.summary: Commission opened Military Attaché Shimanuki's rooms and gave confiscated property to Lieutenant Plujnikov; Fujicenka's effects were returned, clippings and carbon paper burned, film equipment and maps removed.

subfiles.title: List of property removed from the Japanese military attaché’s building
subfiles.from: Allied Control Commission and Romanian officials
subfiles.about: Inventories technical and documentary property seized from the former Japanese military attaché’s building.
subfiles.summary: List of property removed from the Japanese military attaché's building: radio stations, cameras, binoculars, projectors, a typewriter and sealed cases; Plujnikov receipted for the Allied Control Commission depot.

subfiles.title: Statement on opening rooms of the former Japanese Embassy
subfiles.from: Allied Control Commission and Romanian officials
subfiles.about: Records the removal and sealing of property from the former Japanese Embassy on Boulevard Dacia.
subfiles.summary: Statement on opening the former Japanese Embassy rooms: selected property went to the Allied Control Commission depot, the rest sealed in two rooms under Susui; newspapers burned, no objection from former Ambassador Susui.

subfiles.title: Duplicate list of military-attaché property
subfiles.from: Allied Control Commission and Romanian officials
subfiles.about: Provides another copy of the inventory of equipment removed from the Japanese military attaché’s premises.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate list of communications, optical, photographic and office equipment taken from 36 Boulevard A. Constantinescu, with Plujnikov's receipt.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Despatch No. 719
subfiles.from: Burton Y. Berry, U.S. Mission, Bucharest
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report that Japanese premises in Romania were opened but no diplomatic or consular archives survived.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains that Japanese diplomatic buildings were leased and that their archives had been burned before Allied examination. It also notes the sale of most Japanese state property in 1944 and the issue of household goods to interned officials.

subfiles.title: Duplicate statement on the military attaché’s rooms
subfiles.from: Allied Control Commission and Romanian officials
subfiles.about: Duplicates the account of opening Shimanuki’s rooms and removing equipment and maps.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate statement: the attaché's listed property went to Plujnikov, six personal items returned to Fujicenka, papers burned, a projector and map portfolio removed.

subfiles.title: Duplicate inventory of military-attaché property
subfiles.from: Allied Control Commission and Romanian officials
subfiles.about: Lists the technical equipment and sealed documentary containers removed from the military attaché’s building.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate inventory of military-attaché property: radio equipment, cameras, optics, photographic supplies, a typewriter, projectors and three containers of lists.

subfiles.title: Duplicate statement on the former Japanese Embassy
subfiles.from: Allied Control Commission and Romanian officials
subfiles.about: Duplicates the statement on confiscating and sealing property at the Japanese Embassy on Boulevard Dacia.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate statement on the former Japanese Embassy: some property to the Allied Control Commission depot, the rest sealed under Susui, newspapers burned, no objection from Susui.

subfiles.title: Property removed from the former Japanese Embassy
subfiles.from: Allied Control Commission and Romanian officials
subfiles.about: Inventories property removed from the former Japanese Embassy on Boulevard Dacia.
subfiles.summary: Inventory of property removed from the former Japanese Embassy, including literature, gas masks, a periscope, projectors, radios and ten typewriters, receipted by Plujnikov.

subfiles.title: Instructions for joint custody of Japanese property in Siam
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Directs the Legation to organize joint Allied custody and financial control of Japanese official property and funds in Siam.
subfiles.summary: Airgram on Siam: a China, Britain, Soviet and U.S. committee should act with the Siamese Foreign Office, with storage or limited sale of movables, joint trust accounts, rental of real property and necessary custodial or relief spending.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 84 on Japanese premises and archives in Siam
subfiles.doc_type: Incoming telegram, action and information copies
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Bangkok
subfiles.about: Reports destruction of Japanese archives in Bangkok and the status of former diplomatic personnel and provincial consulates.
subfiles.summary: Bombing destroyed the former chancery and consulate-general premises, and remaining records were destroyed on Tokyo’s orders before British forces arrived. Japanese personnel were detained, while consulates at Chiang Mai, Songkhla, and Battambang remained under Siamese police custody pending inventories.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum concerning the British inquiry
subfiles.from: Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Suggests handling or replying to a British inquiry about examination of Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary routing memorandum sending the British question for consideration, preceding the memorandum of Everson's inquiry.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with F. C. Everson
subfiles.from: W. T. Turner, Department of State
subfiles.about: Records a British Embassy inquiry about Allied participation in examining archives in Japan.
subfiles.summary: F. C. Everson asks whether occupation authorities will set up an organization to examine Japanese archives and whether other powers will be invited to take part.

subfiles.title: Circular instructions on Japanese archives
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Expands worldwide instructions for describing, preserving, and examining Japanese diplomatic archives.
subfiles.summary: Missions were asked to assess the existence and intelligence value of Japanese archives and to form interagency working committees where possible. Cryptographic material was to be separated and forwarded, no destruction was to be authorized, and information was to be exchanged with Britain, China, and the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on handling the British archives inquiry
subfiles.from: Hugh Borton, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: States that Foreign Activity Correlation should handle the British request for information from Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Borton has no objection to Cherp's suggestions but notes a January 9 regulation gives Foreign Activity Correlation responsibility for archival requests.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 13,439 requesting transport of Japanese archives
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Renews a recommendation that Japanese official archives in Chile be flown to Washington for examination.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 13,439: the Embassy, which received the archives from the Swedish minister for the Allies, asks the Department to expedite a decision on flying them out by Army aircraft.

subfiles.title: Reply approving shipment of archives from Santiago
subfiles.from: Department of State, James F. Byrnes
subfiles.about: Approves shipment of important Japanese archives to Washington if Allied colleagues agree.
subfiles.summary: State finds shipment of Santiago's archives highly desirable but suggests sending only the most important parts after preliminary examination, not as final disposition, with records available for return.

subfiles.title: Suggestions concerning British participation in archive examination
subfiles.from: P. F. Cherp, Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: Proposes a response to British interest in participating in the examination of archives in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cherp recommends telling Britain information is being sought from Tokyo and asking Atcheson to report; he expects MacArthur to allow limited foreign access, with wider participation possibly needing the Far East Commission.

subfiles.title: Japanese archives and property in Venezuela
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Caracas (William Dawson)
subfiles.about: Reports that the Swiss chargé held no Japanese archives but controlled a Japanese bank account.
subfiles.summary: Venezuela: the Swiss chargé holds no Japanese archives, only a bank account of about 47,000 bolivares.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Central Services
subfiles.about: Identifies the attached white telegram copy as the record copy replacing a missing action copy.
subfiles.summary: Records notice: file the attached copy in place of the unreturned yellow action copy and return it to central records.

subfiles.title: Bern telegram on Swiss transfer of Japanese interests
subfiles.doc_type: Secret incoming telegram, record and action copies
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Bern (Leland Harrison)
subfiles.about: Summarizes Switzerland’s decision to end responsibility for Japanese interests after transferring Japanese property to Allied representatives.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss Government instructed its chargé in Caracas to transfer Japanese property and record that future responsibility rested with the Allied representative. It said the same basis had been used elsewhere, including Argentina, where a January protocol ended Swiss responsibility for Japanese interests.

subfiles.title: Correction to Bern telegram serial number
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Bern
subfiles.about: Corrects the serial number of the Bern telegram from 322 to 304.
subfiles.summary: Correction of the serial number of a Bern secret telegram on Japanese property transfer in Venezuela.

subfiles.title: Report regarding Japanese records, archives, and property in Panama
subfiles.from: Frank T. Hines, U.S. Embassy, Panama
subfiles.about: Reports on Japanese archives, funds, real estate, vehicles, furniture, and proposed disposition of official property in Panama.
subfiles.summary: Panama: the Embassy inventoried and partly copied Japanese archives; Panama and the Alien Property Custodian hold funds and real estate; Hines recommends Panama keep two Packard cars and keep or sell other official property, with proceeds in a Four-Power trust account.

subfiles.title: Follow-up report on Japanese archives in Haiti
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Port-au-Prince (Orme Wilson)
subfiles.about: States that an earlier despatch had already covered the subject of Japanese archives in Haiti.
subfiles.summary: Haiti airgram refers to Secret Despatch 1016 of September 19, 1945, treating the earlier consulate-archives examination as a complete answer to the January 31 circular.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 36: Former Japanese diplomatic and consular property in Siam
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Bangkok (Edwin F. Stanton)
subfiles.about: Reports the status of Japanese property in Siam and the U.S. Legation’s temporary acquisition of a sedan.
subfiles.summary: British authorities supplied an inventory covering Japanese official furniture and personal property, much of which remained in use by detained Japanese personnel. The Legation took custody of a 1941 sedan reportedly connected with the Manchukuo mission, pending clarification of ownership and final policy.

subfiles.title: Inventories of Japanese archives, furnishings, and consular property in Siam
subfiles.from: British and Siamese authorities
subfiles.about: Provides extensive inventories of surviving Japanese records, household goods, office equipment, vehicles, and consular property throughout Siam.
subfiles.summary: Only nine accounting books survived at the Embassy and Consulate General in Bangkok; Chiang Mai and Songkhla held no archives, while Battambang records had gone to Siamese authorities. The inventories enumerate furnishings assigned to named Japanese officials and extensive property at the consulates in Battambang, Songkhla, and Chiang Mai, as well as the Bangkok compound and ambassador’s residence.

subfiles.title: Receipt for vehicle taken over from the Japanese
subfiles.from: American Legation in Siam
subfiles.to: Japanese custodians and Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the American Legation’s receipt of a 1941 sedan formerly in Japanese possession.
subfiles.summary: Receipt for a vehicle taken over from the Japanese, with model year, license and serial numbers, Enclosure 2 to Despatch 36.

subfiles.title: Filing slip for file 894.414/2-1146
subfiles.from: Department of State staff
subfiles.about: Directs that the sheet be filed with the remainder of file 894.414/2-1146.
subfiles.summary: The brief note is purely administrative. It links the following material to the main archival file.

subfiles.title: Unsent draft letter on Japanese archives and property in Canada
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: Ray Atherton, U.S. ambassador in Ottawa
subfiles.about: Explains Allied procedures for Japanese property and proposes joint custody of Japanese assets in Canada.
subfiles.summary: The draft outlines standard policies for preserving archives, storing or selling official property, safeguarding private property, and controlling proceeds through joint trust accounts. Atherton was to discuss early joint custody with the other Allied missions in Ottawa, but the letter is marked “Not Sent.”

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 13,477 transmitting Yamagata’s diary
subfiles.from: Hugh Millard, U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Transmits the second translated portion of former Japanese Minister Yamagata’s diary.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 13,477 sends Yamagata's diary, found in a chest at the Swedish Legation, covering April 1 to July 27, 1942; copy to the British Embassy.

subfiles.title: Some facts in former Japanese Minister Yamagata’s diary
subfiles.from: Yamagata, former Japanese minister to Chile
subfiles.to: Japanese Foreign Ministry and personal diary record
subfiles.about: Records Yamagata’s diplomatic, political, intelligence, propaganda, and financial activities in Chile from April through July 1942.
subfiles.summary: Yamagata described meetings with President Ríos, Chilean officials, Japanese commercial representatives, and German, Italian, Spanish, and Argentine diplomats while monitoring pressure to break with the Axis. He reported intelligence contacts, propaganda work, shipping matters, Socialist agitation, and attempts to obtain or remit money as Chile tightened exchange controls. By July he considered the political situation grave and viewed Tokyo’s order to reprimand the Chilean government as dangerous but unavoidable.
